title: RISC-V: Memory and Program Flow
summary: This unit covers memory accesses in RV32 and shows how bytes, words, strings, arrays, and structs are laid out in memory. You will also practice pointer arithmetic, stack operations, branches, loops, and subroutine calls, including register saving.
concepts: Sign extension and zero extension (Sign Extension und Zero Extension)
Little-endian and big-endian byte order (Little Endian und Big Endian)
Sections and memory layout (Sections und Speicherlayout)
ASCII and C strings (ASCII und C-Strings)
Arrays and pointer arithmetic (Arrays und Pointerarithmetik)
Stack: PUSH and POP (Stack: PUSH und POP)
Conditional branches and branch pseudoinstructions (Bedingte Sprünge und Branch-Pseudoinstruktionen)
Subroutines and register saving (Unterprogramme und Register-Sicherung)
keyFacts: In RV32, registers and pointers are 32 bits wide.
Memory is byte-addressable; `b`, `h`, and `w` denote 1, 2, and 4 bytes, respectively.
The effective address of a load or store instruction is the base register plus a sign-extended immediate.
`lb` and `lh` sign-extend; `lbu` and `lhu` zero-extend by filling the leftmost bits with zeros.
Stores write only the selected lower bits and do not extend the value.
Little-endian order places the least significant byte at the lowest address; big-endian order places the most significant byte there.
`.text` contains executable code; `.data`, `.rodata`, and `.bss` contain global data with different properties.
`.asciz` automatically appends a terminating NULL byte to a string.
A C string ends with NULL; a Pascal string stores its length in a preceding byte.
A pointer contains an address; `la` loads an address, while `lw` loads a word from an address.
In an array, element `i` is `i × sizeof(Element)` bytes beyond the start of the array.
Struct members can have different types; the ERA course simplification ignores padding.
PUSH first decrements `sp` and then writes; POP first reads and then increments `sp`.
A branch jumps when its condition is met; `blt` and `bge` compare signed values, while their u variants compare unsigned values.
`jal` stores the address of the following instruction in `rd`; `jalr` jumps to the register value plus a sign-extended immediate.
When calling a subroutine, save any values that are still needed and restore modified callee-saved registers before returning.
An assembly for loop typically checks the negated termination condition before the body and jumps back after incrementing.

review.notes: 45 Fragen geprüft; Antworten, Distraktoren, Erklärungen, Selbstständigkeit und Rechen-/Code-Verifikationen waren korrekt. Die Quellenüberschrift „jal und jalr“ steht nicht in der erlaubten Überschriftenliste und wurde auf null gesetzt. Keine Fragen entfernt.

questions.prompt: What does `la t0, x` mean in this RV32 example?

options.text: It loads a byte from the address in `x`.
It loads the address of `x` into `t0`.
It loads the value of `x` into `t0`.
It stores `t0` at the address of `x`.

questions.explanation: `la` loads the address of a label. To read the data at that address, you would then need, for example, `lw`.

questions.prompt: The load suffix `h` denotes a halfword of ___ bytes.
questions.explanation: A halfword is 16 bits wide, so it occupies two bytes.

questions.prompt: Which load instructions zero-extend a loaded byte to the register width?
questions.explanation: Here, `u` marks zero extension: `lbu` and `lhu` fill the leftmost bits with zeros. `lb` and `lh` use sign extension.

questions.prompt: In little-endian order, the least significant byte of a multibyte value is at the lowest address.
questions.explanation: Little-endian order places the least significant byte first, at the lowest address of the value.

questions.prompt: What kind of content is stored in the `.rodata` section?
questions.explanation: `.rodata` contains initialized, non-writable global data. Executable code is stored in `.text`.

questions.prompt: The assembler directive `.asciz` automatically appends a terminating ___ to a string.
questions.explanation: `.asciz` stands for ASCII zero and appends a NULL byte at the end.

questions.prompt: ASCII encodes characters using numeric values from 0 to 127.
questions.explanation: The ASCII range used in this unit includes values from 0 to 127.

questions.prompt: How wide is a pointer in the RV32 context used here?
questions.explanation: RV32 uses 32-bit registers and 32-bit pointers.

questions.prompt: Which statements about arrays and structs are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A struct cannot have named members.
Structs group fields that can have different types.
Arrays always store their elements at separate, arbitrary addresses.
Arrays contain elements of the same type.

questions.explanation: Arrays consist of elements of the same type; structs group members that can have different types. The other statements contradict these definitions.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes pushing a 32-bit register onto the stack?
questions.explanation: PUSH uses pre-decrement: first, `sp` is decremented by four bytes; then the register is stored at the new address.

questions.prompt: In the instruction notation, `rd` stands for the ___ register.
questions.explanation: `rd` stands for register destination, meaning the destination register. `rs`, `rs1`, and `rs2` denote source registers.

questions.prompt: A load uses `rs1 = 0x1000` and `imm = -12`. What is the resulting effective address?
questions.explanation: The effective address is the base plus the sign-extended immediate: `0x1000 − 12 = 0x0FF4`.

questions.prompt: A byte with the bit pattern `10000000` is loaded in RV32 using `lb`. What 32-bit pattern is then in the register?
questions.explanation: The byte's most significant bit is 1. `lb` repeats this sign bit up to the register width, producing `0xFFFFFF80`.

questions.prompt: The 32-bit value `0xA1B2C3D4` is stored in little-endian order starting at address `n`. Which bytes appear in the order `n`, `n+1`, `n+2`, `n+3`?
questions.explanation: Little-endian order stores the least significant byte first. Therefore, the bytes at increasing addresses are `D4`, `C3`, `B2`, `A1`.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does `.asciz "RAM"` occupy in memory?
questions.explanation: Each of the three ASCII characters occupies one byte. `.asciz` adds a terminating NULL byte, for a total of four bytes.

questions.prompt: An array of 4-byte elements starts at `0x2000`. At what address is `a[3]`?
questions.explanation: The offset is `3 × 4 = 12` bytes. Thus, `a[3]` is at `0x2000 + 12 = 0x200C`.

questions.prompt:
What are the contents of `t0` and `t1` after this code runs? The label `x` is at `0x200`, where the word `17` is stored.
```asm
la t0, x
lw t1, 0(t0)
```
questions.explanation: `la` loads the address `0x200` into `t0`. `lw` then reads the word at that address into `t1`, so its value is 17.

questions.prompt: A struct is laid out without padding. Its fields, in order, are `int` (4 bytes), `short` (2 bytes), `unsigned int` (4 bytes), and `unsigned char` (1 byte). What is the byte offset of the third field?
questions.explanation: The third field starts after the first two fields: `4 + 2 = 6` bytes from the start of the struct.

questions.prompt: `sp` is `0x7FFC` before a PUSH. The PUSH saves a 32-bit register. What is the value of `sp` immediately after the PUSH?
questions.explanation: A 32-bit register requires four bytes. PUSH first decrements `sp` by 4, so `0x7FFC − 4 = 0x7FF8`.

questions.prompt: `t0 = 0xFFFFFFFF` and `t1 = 1`. Is the branch `blt t0, t1, ziel` taken? Interpret the register values as signed.

options.text: Yes, because `0xFFFFFFFF` is greater as an unsigned value.
No, because the two values are equal.

questions.explanation: `blt` compares signed values. Interpreted as a 32-bit two's-complement value, `0xFFFFFFFF` equals −1; −1 is less than 1, so the branch is taken.

questions.prompt: How is the branch pseudoinstruction `bgt rs1, rs2, label` implemented?
questions.explanation: To express “greater than” using the available `blt` instruction, swap the operands: `rs2 < rs1`.

questions.prompt:
How many times does the body execute, and what value is in `t1` afterward?
```asm
li t0, 1
li a0, 4
li t1, 0
loop:
    bge t0, a0, end
    addi t1, t1, 1
    addi t0, t0, 1
    j loop
end:
```
questions.explanation: The branch ends the loop when `t0 >= 4`. The body runs for `t0 = 1, 2, 3`, so it runs three times; `t1` is incremented three times.

questions.prompt: `t0 = 0xFFFFFFFF` and `t1 = 1`. Which statements about the two comparisons are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `bltu t0, t1, L` branches because `0xFFFFFFFF` is less than 1.
`blt` and `bltu` always interpret the operands in the same way.
`bltu t0, t1, L` does not branch because `0xFFFFFFFF > 1` holds for unsigned values.
`blt t0, t1, L` branches because `−1 < 1` holds for signed values.

questions.explanation: `blt` interprets `0xFFFFFFFF` as signed −1, whereas `bltu` interprets the same bit pattern as a large unsigned number. Therefore, only the signed comparison is true.

questions.prompt: `rs2` contains `0x123456AB`. An `sb rs2, 0(t0)` stores to the address in `t0`. What byte value is written?
questions.explanation: `sb` stores only the lower 8 bits of `rs2`. The least significant byte is `0xAB`.

questions.prompt: Which formula describes the effective address for `lw rd, imm(rs1)`?

options.text: `imm` as an absolute address, independent of `rs1`

questions.explanation: The base address comes from register `rs1`; the sign-extended immediate is added as the offset.

questions.prompt: The target of a conditional branch is encoded relative to the PC; its range is approximately ±4 KiB.
questions.explanation: The branch offset is encoded in the instruction. The stated range is approximately ±4 KiB.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `.bss` are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: It can reserve space for a specified number of bytes.
It is the section for initialized, non-writable global data.
It contains uninitialized, writable global data.

questions.explanation: `.bss` is intended for uninitialized, writable global data and reserves the required space. Code is stored in `.text`, and initialized, non-writable data is stored in `.rodata`.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe PUSH and POP? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: With POP, the stored value is overwritten first and then read.
POP first reads the value and then increments `sp`.
PUSH first decrements `sp` and then writes the value.
In this example, PUSH and POP are each single, newly introduced RV32I machine instructions.

questions.explanation: PUSH is an instruction sequence with pre-decrement, and POP is one with post-increment. Here, these names do not refer to individual additional machine instructions.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish the string formats presented here? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A Pascal string begins with a byte that specifies its length.
A Pascal string must end with NULL to indicate its length.
A C string ends with a terminating NULL byte.
A C string always stores its length in a preceding byte.

questions.explanation: In a C string, a NULL byte marks the end; the Pascal string presented here stores the length in its first byte. The other statements swap these characteristics.

questions.prompt: Which real instruction form corresponds to the unconditional jump `j label`?
questions.explanation: `j label` is `jal x0, label` or `jal zero, label`. The link address is written to `zero` and thus discarded.

questions.prompt: For `jalr ra, t0, -4`, before the instruction: old PC `0x200`, `t0 = 0x800`. What new PC address and return address result?
questions.explanation: `jalr` sets the new PC to `t0 + SignExt(−4) = 0x7FC` and stores `PC_alt + 4 = 0x204` in `ra`.

questions.prompt:
What number is in `t2` at the end?
```asm
li t0, -1
li t1, 1
blt t0, t1, less
li t2, 0
j end
less:
li t2, 1
end:
```

options.text: The code does not branch to `end`.

questions.explanation: `blt` compares signed values. −1 is less than 1, so the code branches to `less` and sets `t2` to 1.

questions.prompt: An assembly instruction `sw a1, 6(a0)` stores a word. Which statement describes this access?

options.text: The 32 bits of `a1` are written to absolute address 6.
The 32 bits of `a1` are written starting at address `a0 + 6`.
The word at `a0` is loaded into `a1`; 6 is the register width.
The lower 16 bits of `a1` are written to address `a0 + 6`.

questions.explanation: For `sw`, `a1` is the source; 32 bits are written to the effective address computed as the base register plus the offset, which here is `a0 + 6`.

questions.prompt: Subroutine A calls B with `jal ra, B`. B then calls C with `jal ra, C` and must return to A afterward. What must B do?

options.text: B must not save `ra` because `jal` automatically stores the old return address on the stack.
B must set `ra` to zero before calling C.
B must save its current return address before calling C and restore it before returning.
B must save C's return address in `x0`.

questions.explanation: The second `jal` overwrites `ra` with the return address within B. B must therefore save the return address to A and restore it later.

questions.prompt: A program has instructions in `.text` and initialized global data in `.data`. Which statement fits the von Neumann model?

options.text: Only data is stored in main memory; instructions exist only in registers.
`.text` and `.data` necessarily denote two separate processors.
Code and data are always stored in separate main memories.
Program code and data are stored in the same main memory.

questions.explanation: In the von Neumann model, programs and data reside in the same main memory. The sections identify different types of content in that memory.

questions.prompt:
A struct is at `0x100`; its pointer field `data` contains `0x200`. At `0x200` are the bytes `0x48`, `0x69`, `0x00` (ASCII “Hi” followed by NULL). The length field begins at offset 4. What value does the code store there?
```asm
lw t0, 0(a0)
li t1, 0
loop:
    lbu t2, 0(t0)
    beq t2, zero, done
    addi t1, t1, 1
    addi t0, t0, 1
    j loop
done:
    sw t1, 4(a0)
```
questions.explanation: The code loads the string pointer and counts bytes until it reads the NULL byte. It counts `0x48` and `0x69`, but not the NULL byte, so it stores 2.

questions.prompt: A word array starts at `0x300` and contains `5`, `8`, and `42` in that order; each element occupies 4 bytes. The code loads `a[2]` using `lw`. What value is read?
questions.explanation: `a[2]` is at `0x300 + 2 × 4 = 0x308`. `lw` loads the data at that address, namely the third word, whose value is 42.

questions.prompt: At address `s0` is the byte `0x80`. The code then executes `lb t0, 0(s0)` and `bge t0, zero, nonnegative`. Is the branch taken?

options.text: No, because `lb` sign-extends the value to −128.
No, because `bge` always compares unsigned values.
Yes, because `0x80` is positive as a signed number.

questions.explanation: `lb` sign-extends `0x80` to `0xFFFFFF80`, which is signed −128. `bge` is signed; −128 is not greater than or equal to zero.

questions.prompt: For `for (int i = a; i < b; ++i)`, the assembler should branch to the label `end` when the termination condition is met. Which statements fit the loop pattern? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: After the body, increment `i` and then jump to the start of the loop.
Before the body, `bge i, b, end` can test the negated loop condition.
The test `i >= b` must run after the increment to allow the first iteration.
`blt i, b, end` ends the loop exactly when `i < b` holds.

questions.explanation: The termination condition is the negation of `i < b`, namely `i >= b`. After the body, increment and jump back to the test.

questions.prompt: An RV32 struct contains `char *data` at offset 0 and `unsigned int length` at offset 4. Which statements are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `sw t1, 4(a0)` can store a calculated length value in the `length` field.
`lw t0, 0(a0)` can load the pointer `data` from the struct.
The length field begins at offset 8.
`lbu t0, 0(a0)` loads the complete 32-bit pointer in one step.

questions.explanation: In the stated layout, both fields are four bytes: the pointer is at offset 0 and the length at offset 4. `lbu` loads only one byte, so it cannot load the complete pointer.

questions.prompt: For `jalr rd, rs, imm`, according to the address calculation used here, `PC_alt + 4` is written to `rd`, and execution jumps to `rs + SignExt(imm)`.
questions.explanation: `jalr` stores the address of the following instruction in `rd` and calculates the jump target as the register value plus the sign-extended immediate.

questions.prompt: For a more distant subroutine, the sequence first shows `___ ra, offset[31:12]` and then `jalr ra, ra, offset[11:0]`.
questions.explanation: The sequence shown uses `auipc` to form the upper part of the offset relative to the PC; `jalr` then handles the lower part.

questions.prompt: In the call sequence shown, which step comes immediately after the caller's preparation?

context.content:
flowchart TD
  A[Caller prepares] --> B[Jump and Link]
  B --> C[Callee works]
  C --> D[Callee finishes]
  D --> E["Return; caller resumes"]
context.caption: Subroutine call sequence

options.text: Jump and Link stores the return address.

questions.explanation: After preparing values and parameters, the subroutine is called with Jump and Link; the return address is stored at that point.

questions.prompt: At which step in the sequence shown are the result and the registers to be restored prepared for the return?

context.content:
flowchart TD
  A[Caller prepares] --> B[Jump and Link]
  B --> C[Callee works]
  C --> D[Callee finishes]
  D --> E["Return; caller resumes"]
context.caption: Subroutine call sequence

questions.explanation: When finishing, the callee stores the result and restores the callee-saved registers it used before returning.

levels.title: Practice: Bytes, Branches, and Aha Moments

questions.prompt: You are rendering an image and reading a color channel as an **unsigned** byte. The memory contains `11100000`; the register should contain the value `224`. Which RV32 instruction loads exactly one byte and zero-extends it?
questions.explanation: `lbu` loads one byte and zero-extends it, so `11100000` is read as `224`. `lb` interprets the set sign bit as a negative sign.

questions.prompt: A network protocol stores a 32-bit field **with the most significant byte first**. At increasing addresses, you see the bytes `12 34 56 78`. Which byte order is being used?
questions.explanation: In big-endian order, the most significant byte is at the lowest address. The order described is therefore big-endian.

questions.prompt: You are working with RV32: pointers are 32 bits wide, and each address identifies one byte. How large is the byte-addressable address space? Use 1 GiB = 2³⁰ bytes.
questions.explanation: A 32-bit pointer can represent 2³² distinct addresses. That gives 2³² ÷ 2³⁰ = 4 GiB of byte-addressable locations.

questions.prompt: A text API receives the bytes `0x4F 0x4B 0x00 0x58` and should stop at the first zero byte. Which string convention fits?

options.text: Pascal string: length stored in the first byte
Word array: terminated by a four-byte zero word
Fixed-length string: length stored only outside the buffer
C string: terminated by a final zero byte

questions.explanation: A C string ends at the first zero byte, here after the characters `OK`. A Pascal string instead stores its length at the beginning.

questions.prompt: A game stores scores in an array of 4-byte values. The array starts at `0x1000`; the index starts at 0. At what address is element `a[6]`?
questions.explanation: Element 6 is 6 × 4 = 24 bytes beyond the start. Its address is therefore `0x1000 + 24 = 0x1018`.

questions.prompt: A game stores 37 measurements in an RV32 word array. A word occupies 4 bytes. How many bytes does the array itself occupy?
questions.explanation: Each array element occupies 4 bytes. In total, that is 37 × 4 = 148 bytes.

questions.prompt: You are building an app with machine code, an immutable label, and a global, writable buffer with no specified initial contents. Which mappings are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `.text` contains executable code, `.rodata` read-only data, and `.bss` uninitialized global data. Therefore, A, B, and C are correct.

questions.prompt: You save five 32-bit registers to the stack in sequence, using one PUSH operation for each. Without additional padding, how many bytes do the saved registers occupy in total?
questions.explanation: A register is 32 bits, or 4 bytes, wide. Five PUSH operations therefore occupy 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.

questions.prompt: A game checks `if (lives == 0) game_over();` and should jump to the end of the game only when there are zero lives. Which RISC-V concept represents this decision?
questions.explanation: A conditional branch jumps only when its condition is met. Here, `beq` can compare the value of `lives` with zero.

questions.prompt: A parser processes nested messages recursively. Before another `jal`, the old return value in `ra` and a local value must still be available after returning. Where does it typically save these values for each call?

options.text: In one shared global variable for all calls
On the heap, which is automatically cleared for each call
On the stack, in a separate call frame
In `.rodata`, because the values should remain unchanged

questions.explanation: A separate stack frame can save the return address and local values for each nested call independently. Another `jal` writes a new return address to `ra`; the old value must be restored if it is needed.
